prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Nike, Arizona, Nogales

outputs.L1:
Among thirty dusty men, the only wet thing is the mouth of the coyote. It is a mini zoo. We are from many countries, in which there are many coyotes. Five hundred bucks and we’re off. Think about it: it is the shortest verse of a corrido.

A Gila monster and a coyote are one. A Gila monster, a coyote, and a gringo are one. Strewn bottles melt into dirt; the coyote’s tongue fills them. We don’t know which to swat: the coyote or the froth, the mosquitoes or the flies.

Gringos, why do you see us as illegal? Don’t you think we are the workers around you? We speak different accents, yours included, and we know también. The coyote is suspicious of what we say.

When the coyote hears helicopters, in Nike shoes he trots Arizona. Nogales whores close their doors. The coyote trots Arizona in Nike shoes. The desert is still. The coyote must be tired. In his shadow, he sees searchlights. It’s day all night. It’s dusting, and it’s going to dust. The coyote rests under yuccas.
outputs.L2:
In a group of thirty men coated with dust, the only damp thing is the coyote’s mouth.  
It is like a tiny zoo: we come from many nations, places where coyotes are common.  
Five hundred dollars, and we begin the trip. Think of that—  
it is the briefest line in a corrido.

A Gila monster and a coyote become the same thing.  
A Gila monster, a coyote, and a gringo become the same thing.  
Scattered bottles soften into the dirt;  
the coyote’s tongue reaches into them.  
We cannot tell what we should slap at—  
the coyote or the foam,  
the mosquitoes or the flies.

Gringos, why do you look at us and call us illegal?  
Don’t you realize we are the laborers surrounding you?  
We speak in many accents, including yours,  
and we know también.

The coyote grows suspicious of our words.  
When he hears helicopters, he runs through Arizona in Nike shoes.  
In Nogales, the whores shut their doors.  
The coyote keeps moving across Arizona in his Nikes.

The desert remains motionless.  
The coyote must be exhausted.  
Inside his own shadow, he imagines searchlights.  
Night is bright as day.  
Dust is falling, and everything is turning to dust.  
The coyote stops to rest beneath the yuccas.
outputs.L3:
Thirty migrants from many different countries travel together through the desert, guided by a coyote after each of them has paid him five hundred dollars. They come from diverse backgrounds and speak with many accents, yet they share the same difficult journey across the harsh Arizona landscape. Their movement through the desert is not only a physical crossing but also a struggle for survival, dignity, and recognition.

The poem presents the coyote in two ways at once. On one level, he is a smuggler, a paid guide who leads migrants across the border illegally. On another level, he is described almost like an animal, blending into the desert environment and moving through it with instinct and endurance. This double image connects him to the wilderness around him, making him seem both human and creature-like as he navigates the dangerous terrain.

The migrants question why they are treated as “illegal.” They see themselves not as criminals, but as workers—people who labor, move, and contribute. They speak in many different accents, including accents that resemble or include those of the “gringos” themselves. This suggests that identity and belonging are more complicated than legal labels. The poem challenges the idea that these migrants are outsiders by showing their humanity, diversity, and connection to the same world as those who reject them.

Their journey through the desert is full of hardship and fear. The Arizona landscape is exhausting and dangerous, filled with heat, insects, trash, and signs of other desperate crossings. The migrants must keep moving despite fatigue and uncertainty. Helicopters, searchlights, and the constant threat of being discovered intensify the atmosphere of fear. The desert becomes both a natural obstacle and a place of surveillance, where the migrants are exposed to danger from the environment and from authorities.

Throughout the poem, the coyote continues forward across Arizona, wearing Nike shoes that connect this harsh journey to the modern, commercial world. His shoes contrast with the ancient desert landscape, emphasizing the strange mixture of survival, capitalism, and migration. In the end, he finally rests under the yuccas, a desert plant that offers some shelter. This final image suggests exhaustion and temporary relief, but it also shows that the journey is ongoing and uncertain, shaped by hardship, movement, and the search for a better life.
outputs.L4:
The text presents migrant border crossing as a violent and disorienting experience, told through a surreal, fragmented narrative that resembles a corrido set in the desert. At the center of this world is the figure of the coyote, a guide who is both necessary and dangerous, someone who helps migrants cross but may also profit from their desperation. The desert becomes more than a landscape; it turns into a space of fear, confusion, thirst, surveillance, and death. Its harshness reflects the cruelty of the border itself, where human beings are reduced to bodies moving through heat, sand, fences, and checkpoints.

Through this fragmented style, the text captures the instability of the migrant experience. The journey is not presented as a simple passage from one country to another, but as a broken and threatening process in which identity, safety, and dignity are constantly under attack. Migrants are hunted, watched, and categorized as “illegal,” even though their movement is driven by poverty, labor demands, and survival. The label of illegality becomes a way to erase their humanity and justify their mistreatment.

The text also exposes the exploitation at the heart of the border system. Migrants are treated as disposable laborers: needed for their work, but rejected as people. They are welcomed when their labor is profitable—in fields, factories, kitchens, construction sites, and other forms of difficult work—but condemned when they seek rights, security, or recognition. This contradiction reveals the hypocrisy of a society that depends on migrant labor while criminalizing the migrants themselves.

The figure of the coyote helps reveal this larger system of exploitation. While the coyote may appear as an individual smuggler or trickster, he also represents the broader forces that shape migration: economic inequality, militarized borders, racism, and the demand for cheap labor. Migrants must rely on coyotes because legal and safe routes are often closed to them. Their vulnerability is not accidental; it is produced by a system that makes crossing dangerous and then blames migrants for attempting it.

The text’s surreal and corrido-like qualities intensify its political message. Like a border ballad, it remembers suffering, movement, and resistance, while its fragmented form mirrors the trauma of displacement. Images of the desert, the coyote, surveillance, prejudice, and labor come together to show how the border dehumanizes those who cross it. Yet the text also insists on the humanity of migrants. Beneath the labels and stereotypes are workers, families, travelers, and survivors.

Ultimately, the text condemns the human cost of border systems. It shows that migrants are not criminals by nature, but people made vulnerable by laws, economies, and prejudices that depend on their labor while denying their dignity. By portraying the border as both a physical and symbolic space of exploitation, the narrative challenges readers to see beyond the word “illegal” and recognize the lives, risks, and sacrifices hidden behind it.

Nike has a strong presence across Arizona, where sports, fitness, and outdoor lifestyles are part of everyday life. From major cities like Phoenix and Tucson to border communities such as Nogales, Arizona, Nike products are popular among athletes, students, and people who enjoy staying active.

Nogales, located on the U.S.–Mexico border, is a unique city with a rich cultural mix and a strong sense of community. In a place where soccer, running, basketball, and school athletics are important, Nike shoes, apparel, and sports gear are often associated with performance and style. Many residents and visitors look for comfortable footwear and activewear that can handle both daily routines and athletic activities.

Arizona’s warm climate also makes lightweight and breathable sportswear especially useful. Whether someone is training outdoors, walking through downtown Nogales, or participating in local sports events, Nike offers products designed for comfort, durability, and movement. In this way, Nike connects with the active spirit of Arizona and the vibrant community of Nogales.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about migrants crossing the Arizona desert with a coyote guide, incorporating corrido-like rhythms, Spanglish, border imagery, helicopters, Nike shoes, mosquitoes, and the phrase “we are from many countries.”
counterfactuals.output:
We walked where the moon had a cracked guitar,  
where the saguaro lifted its many arms like saints  
too tired to bless us.

Órale, said the coyote, rápido, bajito,  
and his shadow went ahead of him,  
sniffing the dark for Border Patrol,  
for la migra, for the white teeth of headlights  
biting the wash.

Our Nike shoes drank dust.  
Our tongues carried little deserts.  
In our pockets: a mother’s prayer,  
a photo folded like a wounded bird,  
two pesos, three quetzales, a key  
to a door already far behind.

We are from many countries,  
said the man with the blue bandana.  
We are from many countries,  
said the woman holding her child’s sleep  
against her chest.  
And the desert answered in rattles,  
in thorns, in stars nailed bright  
to the black wooden sky.

Ay, frontera, frontera,  
thin line of wire and rumor,  
you cut the night in two  
but the night keeps bleeding through.

Above us, helicopters chopped the air  
into pieces of silver tortilla.  
Their lights swept the ground  
like a giant searching for a lost coin,  
and we became stones, shrubs, bones,  
became anything that could not be deported.

Mosquitoes sang corridos in our ears:  
de Honduras, de Oaxaca, de Haití, de Zacatecas,  
un paso, otro paso, no mires atrás.  
They drank from us like tiny officials  
stamping our skin with red visas.

The coyote lifted his hand.  
Even the darkness stopped walking.  
Somewhere a fence glittered—  
not a fence, but a harp of knives,  
playing the song of aquí no, aquí no.

Still we moved.

Con los pies ampollados,  
with blistered hope,  
with the desert inside our shoes  
and the sky inside our mouths,  
we followed the coyote’s whisper  
through mesquite, through checkpoint dreams,  
through the land where bones bloom white  
after rain.

And if dawn found us,  
it found us singing softly,  
not because we were unafraid,  
but because fear too has a rhythm:

camina, hermano, camina,  
la noche es larga pero no eterna,  
we are from many countries,  
and the sun, that old burning witness,  
rose over Arizona  
like a coin no one could spend.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental, punctuation-light poem in a Latinx borderlands voice where the “coyote” is both animal and smuggler, set near Nogales, with references to gringos, 500 bucks, Gila monsters, dusty men, and desert exhaustion.
counterfactuals.output:
near Nogales the fence hums like a bad tooth

coyote slips under moonlight  
four legs then two  
fur then denim  
eyes gold then tired

he says 500 bucks  
and points with his chin  
past the wash  
past the mesquite  
past where gringos leave water jugs  
and prayers gone warm

dusty men follow  
their names tucked under tongues  
their mothers tucked under ribs  
one carries a plastic bag of pan dulce  
flat as a map

Gila monsters dream in the rocks  
pink black ancient  
too slow to be afraid  
too holy to explain

the desert says  
drink  
then takes the word back

coyote laughs without laughing  
animal throat  
human debt  
he knows every star by bruise  
every siren by hunger

Nogales glows behind us  
a necklace broken in two countries

the gringos sleep cold  
in houses with sprinklers

we keep walking  
sand in the teeth  
sun waiting like a cop  
exhaustion climbing our backs  
with its little claws

coyote stops  
sniffs the air  
counts us again

one shadow short

nobody says milagro  
nobody says lost

only the desert  
opening its dry mouth  
and the coyote  
answering  
yes  
yes  
keep moving
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a fragmented political poem about undocumented workers and the U.S.-Mexico border, using long breathless lines, minimal punctuation, and images of bottles, dirt, froth, yuccas, searchlights, and helicopters.
counterfactuals.output:
at the edge of the map someone leaves a bottle in the dirt and calls it mercy  

someone else calls it evidence  

the border keeps breathing through its chain teeth through its floodlights through the dry mouths of yuccas standing like witnesses with their arms full of knives  

and the workers come with names folded small in their pockets with phone numbers fading from sweat with the moon on their shoulders and the helicopters beating the sky into froth  

no one is illegal when the fields are thirsty  

no one is illegal when the kitchens want hands before dawn when the fruit hangs heavy and obedient when the cities shine because someone unseen has scrubbed the night from their floors  

but the searchlights arrive like white questions  

but the radios crackle  

but the desert keeps every footprint until the wind is ordered to forget  

a mother pours the last warm bottle cap of water into her child’s mouth and the dirt drinks what spills  

a man kneels by a yucca not to pray but because his legs have become another country  

above him the helicopter circles and circles making a border of sound  

below him the earth is brown and open and older than papers older than patrols older than the word trespass  

listen  

the bottles are crushed in the sun  

the froth of fear gathers at the lips of the nation  

the dirt remembers the bodies it was asked to hide  

and still hands move north through thorn and dust through wages and hunger through the long breathless corridor between need and blame  

still they carry tomatoes roofs children songs  

still they cross because bread is a law too  

because love has no checkpoint  

because the yuccas bloom white in the dark like small explosions of refusal  

because every searchlight fails somewhere  

because every border is finally a line drawn through a human throat
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem in the style of contemporary border-crossing poetry: surreal, compressed, and angry, featuring migrants questioning why gringos call them illegal, a coyote in Nike shoes, and the Arizona desert becoming “day all night.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Day All Night**

Why do the gringos call us illegal,  
as if hunger signed a law,  
as if thirst crossed first  
with fake papers?

The moon is a torn tortilla.  
The fence hums its metal psalm.  
A coyote in Nike shoes  
counts our shadows like money,  
says walk faster,  
says don’t cough your mother’s name.

Behind us: the country  
with its mouth full of smoke.  
Ahead: the country  
with its mouth full of dogs.

We carry water,  
saints,  
phone numbers dissolving in sweat.  
We carry the dead  
who are not yet dead,  
their bones already learning English  
under the sand.

Why illegal?  
says the boy with cactus needles  
in his sleeve.  
Was the river illegal  
when it bent?  
Was the corn illegal  
when it crossed inside our blood?  
Was my grandmother illegal  
praying to a sky  
with no passport?

Arizona opens its furnace-eye.  
The desert becomes day all night.  
Even the stars look like patrol lights.  
Even God keeps his hands up.

And still we move—  
not ghosts, not numbers,  
not the bad dream of a border guard,  
but people,  
people,  
people,

with blistered feet  
kicking at the locked door  
of morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde corrido/prose-poem about thirty men being led through the desert by a coyote, mixing English and Spanish, with repeated lines about “the coyote trots Arizona” and imagery of Nogales, whores, flies, mosquitoes, and dust.
counterfactuals.output:
**Corrido del Coyote que Trota Arizona**

Treinta hombres cruzan la noche como si la noche fuera una herida,  
treinta sombras con la lengua llena de polvo,  
treinta nombres doblados en el bolsillo,  
treinta santos sin vela, sin agua, sin señal.

Y adelante va el coyote—  
no lobo, no hombre, no guía,  
sino una raya negra contra la luna caliente.

**The coyote trots Arizona.**  
**El coyote trota Arizona.**  
**The coyote trots Arizona.**

Nogales quedó atrás con sus focos amarillos,  
sus cantinas con música rota,  
sus putas pintándose la boca contra el espejo de la frontera,  
sus calles oliendo a cerveza, gasolina, miedo.  
Nogales: una moneda mordida por dos países.  
Nogales: where the fence sings in metal teeth.  
Nogales: madre de polvo, padre de alambre.

Treinta hombres caminan.  
Uno lleva una foto de su niña.  
Uno lleva un rosario.  
Uno lleva el número de un primo en Phoenix.  
Uno no lleva nada,  
porque el hambre no cabe en la mochila  
y la esperanza pesa más que el agua.

**The coyote trots Arizona.**  
**El coyote trota Arizona.**  
**The coyote trots Arizona.**

Flies in the mouth of dawn.  
Mosquitos whining like tiny border patrol radios.  
Moscas en los ojos, zumbidos en la sangre,  
the desert scratching its dry nails  
over the backs of the men.

El polvo se les mete en los dientes,  
en el sueño,  
en la idea de Dios.  
Dust becomes bread.  
Dust becomes prayer.  
Dust becomes the mother tongue of the lost.

El coyote dice:  
“Caminen. No miren atrás.  
No prendan luz. No hablen fuerte.  
La migra tiene ojos de buitre.”  
Y los treinta hombres obedecen  
porque el desierto no perdona discursos,  
porque la sed es un patrón antiguo,  
because hunger signs the contract before the body does.

**The coyote trots Arizona.**  
**El coyote trota Arizona.**  
**The coyote trots Arizona.**

En el filo de la madrugada,  
las piedras parecen calaveras.  
Las choyas levantan sus brazos de espinas  
como monjas locas bajo la luna.  
The saguaros stand like witnesses  
too tall to testify.

Treinta hombres:  
not numbers, no,  
not cargo, no,  
not shadows for the evening news—  
treinta corazones golpeando  
contra la puerta cerrada del norte.

Uno se cae.  
Otro lo levanta.  
Uno vomita pura bilis y polvo.  
Otro le da el último trago.  
Uno maldice al coyote.  
Otro maldice a los gobiernos.  
Otro no maldice a nadie:  
he saves his breath for walking.

**The coyote trots Arizona.**  
**El coyote trota Arizona.**  
**The coyote trots Arizona.**

Atrás quedaron las mujeres de Nogales,  
las whores laughing under neon,  
the cheap perfume, the jukebox coughing rancheras,  
las moscas dormidas en el borde de los vasos,  
the border’s dirty halo.  
Atrás quedó la ciudad  
como una boca que no quiso decir adiós.

Ahora sólo hay arena,  
and the moon like a burned tortilla,  
and the coyote’s back moving, moving,  
un punto negro abriendo la herida del camino.

Treinta hombres atraviesan  
un mapa que no los nombra.  
Treinta hombres llevan el sur en los hombros  
y el norte como fiebre en la frente.

**The coyote trots Arizona.**  
**El coyote trota Arizona.**  
**The coyote trots Arizona.**

Ay, corrido sin guitarra,  
corrido de suelas partidas,  
corrido de mosquitos bebiendo sangre migrante,  
corrido de polvo levantado por pies que no salen en la historia.

Sing it low:  
que no los oiga la noche.  
Sing it dry:  
que no se gaste el agua.  
Sing it crooked:  
como la línea que partió la tierra.

Treinta hombres siguen.  
The desert listens.  
El coyote no canta.  
Arizona abre su garganta.

And still—

**the coyote trots Arizona.**  
**el coyote trota Arizona.**  
**the coyote trots Arizona.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
